vignette: The dust rises in thick, ochre clouds as the convoy turns onto the unpaved road. She is thirty-two, clutching her youngest child while her husband guides her through the crowd. The sky darkens too quickly, not with rain, but with exhaust and the distant thud of artillery. She learns to walk without looking back, to swallow the cry that catches in her throat when the children stumble. In the holding camp, nights stretch into something without end. She counts the footsteps of guards above her cot, measures her breathing against sudden cracks echoing through corrugated metal. Trust becomes a luxury she cannot afford. She remembers the call to prayer echoing over the tents, the way her mother’s voice used to steady her. Now she folds the refugee permit with hands that refuse to stop trembling. Now at fifty-five, she stands in a cramped suburban kitchen, wrench in hand, listening to a compressor that refuses to cool. She wipes her forehead with a grease-stained sleeve, feeling the familiar tightness across her ribs. The work is physical, demanding, but it gives her hands a reason to move. She arrives in this country with two suitcases and a divorce that leaves her with nothing but a name and a stubborn refusal to wait for rescue. For years, she learns the language of refrigerants and electrical diagrams, trading the weight of uncertainty for the predictable resistance of copper tubing. When a street outside erupts in the staccato rhythm of a backfiring truck, her body answers before her mind can catch up. She drops the multimeter, presses her palms flat against the cabinets, and waits for an impact that never comes. Her heart hammers against her sternum. She breathes in shallow pulls. At work, she routes around older buildings with exposed fire escapes, preferring new construction where ceilings are flat and alarms stay silent. She keeps her phone screen-up on her hip, because looking down feels like inviting something to strike without warning. Neighbors wave. She waves back, but her smile never reaches her eyes. She stops attending community gatherings after the third one, when sudden applause sends her out the back door, hands shaking, until her pulse slows. Sleep arrives in fragments. She wakes at 3:17 a.m., convinced she hears gravel crunching under boots on the roof. She does not check the windows. She knows she will see only darkness, only the quiet she learned to survive by ignoring. When her ex-husband calls from overseas, his voice carries the cadence of a different life, and she lets it ring until the voicemail catches it. She drinks water from a tall glass on the counter and walks the perimeter of her yard. Her work boots are always scuffed, laces pulled tight. She moves through her days with the careful economy of someone who knows how easily peace can unravel. When she climbs the ladder to adjust a condenser on a rooftop, she feels the wind against her face and watches the horizon with that same steady, watchful gaze. The city stretches below, breathing in traffic and summer heat. She turns back to the unit, flips the disconnect switch, and listens to the machinery settle. She stays a few minutes longer, letting the vibration of the motors travel up through her boots, grounding her, one cycle at a time.
